name: July 2012 Near-Miss CME

phenomena.details: The July 23 eruption from AR 11520 – by then on the Sun's far side – had an estimated soft X-ray class of ~X2.5 (Gopalswamy et al. 2016); the same region produced an X1.4 flare on July 12 while still Earth-facing.
Extreme CME ~2500 km/s; passed through the point of Earth's orbit ~1 week after Earth had moved on. Detected by STEREO-A spacecraft.
Extreme SEP event detected by STEREO-A and ACE; proton flux orders of magnitude above normal.

impacts.description: Modeling studies estimate that if the CME had struck Earth, it would have driven a geomagnetic storm comparable to or exceeding the Carrington Event, with peak Dst estimated at −1182 nT. Direct economic losses could have exceeded $2.6 trillion in the US alone with 1–2 year recovery time.

STEREO-A, which was at the point of Earth's orbit leading Earth by ~120°, directly measured the CME's magnetic field: Bz reached −60 nT sustained for several hours – a configuration that would have been catastrophic for Earth's magnetosphere.

papers.title: A major solar eruptive event in July 2012: Defining extreme space weather scenarios
papers.authors: Baker, D. N., Li, X., Pulkkinen, A., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Characterized the July 23, 2012 CME as a Carrington-class event based on STEREO-A in-situ measurements; estimated that if Earth-directed, it would have driven Dst ~ −1182 nT.

papers.title: On the probability of occurrence of extreme space weather events
papers.keyFinding: Calculated the probability of a Carrington-class event occurring within a decade at approximately 12%, using extreme value statistics.

papers.title: Sun-to-Earth characteristics of the 2012 July 23 ultra-fast transit solar storm
papers.authors: Liu, Y. D., Luhmann, J. G., Kajdič, P., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Reconstructed the full solar-to-Earth propagation characteristics of the July 23 CME, finding it was preceded by a 'clearing' CME on July 19 that reduced the ambient solar wind density and allowed the July 23 CME to maintain its extreme speed.

summary: The July 23, 2012 CME – traveling at ~2500 km/s with an in-situ Bz of −60 nT at STEREO-A – was a Carrington-class solar superstorm that narrowly missed Earth by approximately one week, with modeling estimates suggesting it would have caused over $2.6 trillion in damage to global infrastructure.
description: On July 23, 2012, active region AR 11520 – which was facing Earth just one week earlier – erupted with an extreme coronal mass ejection traveling at approximately 2500 km/s. Because Earth had moved on in its orbit, the CME passed through the point where Earth had been without striking our planet. STEREO-A, a NASA spacecraft positioned approximately 120° ahead of Earth in its orbit, was struck directly and measured the event in unprecedented detail. The in-situ solar wind data revealed a peak magnetic field southward component (Bz) of −60 nT sustained for hours – a configuration that, if directed at Earth, would have driven a storm rivaling or exceeding the 1859 Carrington Event. Baker et al. (2013) estimated the resulting Dst would have been approximately −1182 nT, and insurance and economic modeling placed potential losses at $1–2.6 trillion in the United States alone. The event is now a central reference point in government and industry space weather preparedness planning.
